source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Climactic Reversals: A Spike Followed by a Spike in the Opposite Direction

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode unless noted; a 'climax' is mechanized as a large-range trend bar (or short run of them) relative to recent range/ATR, since the book gives no fixed multiple

candidates.name: ClimaxBar
candidates.quote: Any trend bar or series of trend bars where the bar or bars have relatively large ranges are climaxes... A climax ends as soon as there is any interruption of the strong trending behavior.
candidates.description: Primitive: a trend bar whose range is large relative to recent bars (a multiple of average true range) qualifies as a climax bar, whichever direction it closes.
candidates.pseudocode: (close[0] > open[0] || close[0] < open[0]) && (high[0] - low[0]) >= climaxRangeMultiple * average(trueRange, lookback)
notes: Brooks gives no fixed multiple; 'maybe twice the size of many of the bear trend bars' (page 140) is the closest he comes to a number, used as the default.

candidates.name: ClimaxEndsAtPauseBar
candidates.quote: A climax ends as soon as there is any interruption of the strong trending behavior, such as the formation of a pause bar or a reversal bar.
candidates.description: A run of climax bars in one direction ends at the first following bar that does NOT itself qualify as a same-direction climax bar (a doji, opposite-body bar, or small trend bar).

complexity.reason: one bar's classification compared against the previous bar's

candidates.name: SpikeFollowedByOppositeSpike
candidates.quote: When there is a large spike and it is followed either immediately or soon thereafter by a spike in the opposite direction, the market is trying to reverse... it creates a climactic reversal.
candidates.description: A climax bar in one direction is followed, within a few bars, by a climax bar in the opposite direction. This is the chapter's title concept and the core climactic-reversal trigger. Long side: a bear climax bar occurs, then within N bars a bull climax bar closes -- treat the bull climax bar's close as the reversal signal (enter next open).
candidates.pseudocode: existsClimaxBar(V04-01, direction=down, within=withinBars) && climaxBar(V04-01) && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context signal; the actual entry is the close-then-next-open of the second climax bar)

complexity.reason: requires remembering a recent opposite-direction climax bar plus the current bar's own classification

notes: Same idea as V03-09 (OppositeLargeSpikePairSignalsRange) from Chapter 3, restated here as the chapter's central topic; dedup pass should merge, keeping this chapter's framing since it is the canonical source.

candidates.name: ReversalSpikeSizeExceedsTrendSpike
candidates.quote: The reversal spike can be smaller or larger than the trend spike, and if it is larger, the odds of a reversal are greater.
candidates.description: Given a spike-then-opposite-spike pair (V04-03), the odds of an actual trend reversal (rather than just a pause) are higher when the reversal spike's total range exceeds the original trend spike's range by some margin.

complexity.reason: a stored prior range compared against the current spike's range

candidates.name: ConsecutiveClimaxWithoutPause
candidates.quote: Both bulls and bears will sell when there is a second or third consecutive buy climax without much of a correction between the climaxes, and this selling can lead to a climactic reversal... Two consecutive buy climaxes create two pushes up and is effectively a double top... Three consecutive buy climaxes is a wedge top.
candidates.description: Count same-direction climax bars (V04-01) separated only by small pause bars (not full opposite corrections). The Nth consecutive climax (2 = double top/bottom, 3 = wedge top/bottom) with minimal correction between climaxes raises the odds of at least a 10-bar, two-legged reversal.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context signal feeding an entry at the close of the qualifying climax bar)

complexity.reason: a persistent counter across climax/pause bar classifications with a tunable pause tolerance

notes: The book repeats this pattern (2nd/3rd consecutive climax => reversal odds rise) across several chart examples (AAPL, SPY, Emini); this is one of the chapter's two or three most important mechanizable ideas.

candidates.name: PauseBarOvershootStillCountsAsFinalFlag
candidates.quote: The pause bar sometimes has a high that is slightly above the high of the second buy climax bar, but still acts as a one-bar final flag and leads to a reversal after the third climax.
candidates.description: Tolerance refinement for V04-05: the pause bar between climaxes may overshoot the prior climax's extreme by a small margin and still count as a valid (non-resetting) pause.

complexity.reason: a small fixed-tick tolerance added to an already-hard counting rule

candidates.name: VolumeAndRangeClimaxSpike
candidates.quote: if there is a bull spike with 10 to 20 times the average volume and a range that is five or more times larger than most bars of recent days, the odds are good that there will be higher prices over the next many bars.
candidates.description: A spike bar whose own volume is far above its recent average AND whose range is far above recent average range signals a favorable odds of continuation to at least a measured move (a WITH-trend strength signal, distinct from the fade-the-exhaustion candidates below).
candidates.pseudocode: volume[0] >= volumeMultiple * average(volume, lookback) && (high[0] - low[0]) >= rangeMultiple * average(trueRange, lookback)

complexity.reason: two rolling-average comparisons on the bar's own OHLCV

notes: The volume half is close to VolumeAboveAverageMultiple in the main catalog; kept as a joint volume+range test since the book states both together as the condition for the higher-odds continuation.

candidates.name: ExhaustionBarAfterProtractedTrendWithoutPullback
candidates.quote: when a bull trend goes on for 40 bars without much of a pullback and then has the biggest bull trend bar of the trend... the odds of follow-through buying are less than with all of the other breakouts earlier in the trend... the chance of success is probably less than 30 percent.
candidates.description: If the current trend bar is the largest trend bar of the entire trend so far, AND the trend has run at least N bars without a significant pullback, treat this strongest-looking breakout as more likely to be exhaustion (fade it) rather than a continuation.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (fade filter -- flips the usual with-trend breakout-follow bias)

complexity.reason: needs a persisted trend start point, a 'largest bar of the trend so far' running max, and a 'no significant pullback' tracker

notes: This is the chapter's clearest statement of its core thesis ('sometimes the strongest breakout attempts are the most likely to fail'); worth prioritizing in the authoring pass despite the complexity.

candidates.name: ChannelLineBreakoutFailsWithinBars
candidates.quote: most trend channel line breakouts fail within about five bars and the market then reenters the channel and usually pokes through the opposite side of the channel
candidates.description: After price breaks out beyond a trend channel line, if it closes back inside the channel within N bars, expect it to continue through and poke the opposite trend line rather than resume the breakout direction.
candidates.pseudocode: brokeChannelLine[k] (for some k <= failBars) && close[0] back inside channel

complexity.reason: requires trend-channel-line projection from pivots, on top of a bar-count window

notes: Builds on V02-21 TrendChannelLineOvershootReversal by adding the specific ~5-bar failure window.

candidates.name: TrendChannelLineBreakStrengthensTrend
candidates.quote: The break of a trend line means that a possible trend reversal is underway, but breaking a trend channel line means that the trend has increased in strength and is now steeper.
candidates.description: Classify a break of the (outer) trend channel line as a WITH-trend strengthening signal, opposite in implication to a break of the (inner) trend line, which signals a possible reversal. Used to route the same 'line break' event into the correct filter (V03-01 vs. this one) depending on which line was broken.
candidates.pseudocode: brokeTrendChannelLine(0) => favor with-trend entries, not reversal setups

complexity.reason: requires distinguishing trend-line breaks from trend-channel-line breaks, both needing pivot/line projection

candidates.name: StopSizedToClimaxBarHeight
candidates.quote: they should use a stop that is about as many ticks as the bull trend bar is tall... The aggressive, experienced bulls who bought at the close of bar 15 could have used a protective stop equal to about the height of the bar, which was four points.
candidates.description: When entering at the close of a climax bar (fading it, with-trend), size the initial protective stop to roughly the climax bar's own high-low range rather than a fixed dollar amount or generic ATR multiple.
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop placed at entry price minus/plus the signal bar's own range

complexity.reason: reads one recorded bar's range at entry time and holds it as the stop distance for the trade

candidates.name: InsideBarAfterBreakoutPrecedesReversal
candidates.quote: An inside bar after a breakout bar is often soon followed by a trend bar in the opposite direction, creating a climactic reversal setup.
candidates.description: A breakout trend bar immediately followed by an inside bar, and then a trend bar in the opposite direction, is a climactic-reversal entry trigger (mechanized close-then-next-open on the third bar's close).
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the opposite-direction trend bar, mechanized as its close then next bar's open

complexity.reason: a fixed 3-bar pattern (breakout bar, inside bar, opposite trend bar) with a prior breakout classification

candidates.name: PreferSecondEntryAfterClimaxOverFirstReversal
candidates.quote: it is a more profitable strategy to buy a higher low after a sell climax than it is to buy the initial reversal up, because too many reversal attempts fail. If a second entry fails, the old trend will likely run for at least two more legs.
candidates.description: Block the very first countertrend reversal bar after a climax from being an entry; require a pullback and a second entry (e.g., a higher low) before taking the countertrend trade.
candidates.pseudocode: climaxReversalBar(0) && !isSecondEntry(0) => suppress entry; wait for isSecondEntry

complexity.reason: needs a 'second entry' primitive (a repeat test forming a higher low / lower high)

notes: Close to V02-20 SecondReversalSignal; kept because this chapter states the reward-for-waiting reasoning explicitly (old trend runs 2+ more legs if the second entry also fails).

candidates.name: SteepChannelTestUnreliableForCountertrend
candidates.quote: When a channel is steep, it is a losing strategy to buy every reversal from a trend channel line overshoot. Instead wait until there is a strong breakout of the channel... and then look to buy the breakout pullback.
candidates.description: In a steep channel, suppress countertrend trend-channel-line-overshoot entries; wait instead for a confirmed breakout of the channel and then a breakout-pullback entry.
candidates.pseudocode: channelSteepness(currentChannel) >= steepnessThreshold => suppress trendChannelLineOvershoot entries until channelBreakoutConfirmed

complexity.reason: same undefined 'steep channel' metric flagged in V03-08; restated here specifically for trend-channel-line overshoots

notes: Duplicate of V03-08 SteepChannelTestBlocksReversal in spirit; dedup pass should merge across chapters 3 and 4.

candidates.name: MeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: it spiked down to bar 15 in about a measured move (using the height of the bars 12 to 14 wedge)... a failed wedge usually runs about the height of the wedge as a minimum, creating a great short entry for the measured move down.
candidates.description: Project a profit target equal to the height (high-to-low range) of a prior pattern (spike, wedge, or trading range), added beyond the breakout point in the breakout's direction.
candidates.pseudocode: targetPrice = breakoutPrice + patternHeight (long) / breakoutPrice - patternHeight (short); where patternHeight = highestHigh(patternWindow) - lowestLow(patternWindow)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (profit-target computation, not itself an order type)

complexity.reason: needs the prior pattern's start/end identified by swing-pivot detection before its height can be measured

notes: Recurs constantly across both this chapter and Chapter 3 as 'a measured move up/down'; a high-value target primitive for the authoring pass even though it is hard to build.

candidates.name: WithTrendSpikeSkipsTestRequirement
candidates.quote: A spike pullback does not have to get tested since traders agree that the trend is resuming... but a spike reversal usually gets tested because it is countertrend and traders are less willing to believe that a reversal will succeed.
candidates.description: Classify a spike by whether its direction agrees with (pullback) or opposes (reversal) the prevailing trend. With-trend spikes need no retest before assuming resumption; countertrend spikes should be required to get a retest (V03-03/04 style) before being treated as a real reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: spikeDirection == trendDirection => requireTest = false; else requireTest = true

complexity.reason: needs a trend-direction read plus the spike's own direction; no pivot math beyond that

candidates.name: WedgeReversalRequiresPriorTrendLineBreakAndSecondEntry
candidates.quote: When a wedge is a reversal, it is a countertrend trade and you should wait for a higher low before buying, and only after there has been a strong break of a trend line. Trying to scalp longs in a strong bear trend is a losing strategy.
candidates.description: A wedge-shaped bottom (or top) in a strong opposing trend should be treated as a genuine reversal setup -- not just a with-trend pullback -- only if (a) there was already a strong break of the trend line, and (b) the entry is a second entry (a higher low for a bottom / lower high for a top), not the first wedge signal.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gate on an existing wedge-pattern entry)

complexity.reason: wedge pattern recognition plus trend-line break plus second-entry test, all pivot-dependent

notes: The wedge pattern itself is assumed defined elsewhere (Chapter 7-style three-push pattern); this candidate only captures the added gating condition.

candidates.name: ChannelStartLevelRetestExpectation
candidates.quote: The start of the channel usually gets tested within a day or two.
candidates.description: The price level where a channel began (the spike-to-channel transition point) is likely to be revisited within roughly one to two days; can be used as a magnet/target level for later trades, though the book gives no strict bar count.
candidates.pseudocode: channelStartLevel is likely to be touched again within retestBars

parameters.retestBars: undefined -- 'a day or two', needs a session-length-dependent bar count

complexity.reason: needs a recorded channel-start level plus a decision on how to convert 'a day or two' into a bar count across timeframes

rejected.quote: the Globex 1 minute Emini spiked up on a 5:30 a.m. PST report
rejected.reason: attributes the spike to a scheduled news report; the engine has no news-calendar input

rejected.quote: There are usually tick and oscillator divergences as well... a volume divergence at the low... There probably was a tick divergence and divergences on many oscillators as well
rejected.reason: tick-level divergence data below the bar is not available to the engine

rejected.quote: Was it more likely due to shorting by the institutions... or was it due to aggressive buying by both the bulls and the bears... Other institutions are selling as part of a hedge in another market
rejected.reason: infers a specific market participant's identity and motive behind a volume bar; not decidable from OHLCV

chapter_summary: Chapter 4 defines a climax broadly (any large-range trend bar) and argues that a climactic reversal is simply a spike followed, soon, by an opposite spike -- a failed breakout, mechanized here as ClimaxBar (V04-01) and SpikeFollowedByOppositeSpike (V04-03). The chapter's most distinctive, non-Chapter-2 content is the consecutive-climax counting logic (V04-05/06: 2 climaxes = double top/bottom, 3 = wedge, each raising the odds of a 10-bar two-legged correction), the volume+range spike-strength filter (V04-07), the 'strongest breakout of a protracted trend is often the exhaustion, not the continuation' thesis (V04-08), the measured-move target primitive (V04-15, recurring constantly in both this chapter and Chapter 3), and a concrete stop-sizing rule (V04-11: stop = the climax bar's own height). Several ideas (V04-09/10/14/16/18) either extend Chapter 3's trend-line/channel-line material or restate its 'steep channel = don't fade' and 'spike pullback vs. spike reversal, which gets tested' themes and should be deduped against V03-08 and V03-09 specifically. About two-thirds of the chapter is 17 fully worked chart examples (AAPL, ES/Emini, GS, SPY, RIMM, SKF, OIH) illustrating this same handful of ideas plus Chapter 2/3 primitives (double tops/bottoms, wedges, ii patterns, second entries, one-bar final flags) rather than introducing new mechanizable statements; the mining above focuses on the general statements, not the per-bar walkthroughs. Volume/tick divergence and news-driven moves were rejected as outside the engine's inputs.
